fetched_contents.text: High microplastic pollution in birds of urban waterbodies revealed by non-invasively collected faecal samples 1. Introduction Plastic waste ultimately concentrates in aquatic environments, where it is ingested or absorbed by wildlife (Bhatt and Chauhan, 2023). In birds, plastic particles have been identified in hundreds of aquatic and terrestrial species (Wang et al., 2021). Microplastics are commonly ingested by birds with their food (de Souza et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Carrillo et al., 2023) or by inhalation (Tokunaga et al., 2023). The ingestion of microplastic particles can have toxicological effects on birds, e.g. by negatively affecting immune responses and gut microbiota (Fackelmann et al., 2023; Jing et al., 2024), by causing liver inflammation (Yin et al., 2023a, Yin et al., 2023b) or by damaging lung tissue (Lu et al., 2023, Lu et al., 2024), and ultimately leads to reduced growth rates (Monclús et al., 2022) and decreased body condition (de Souza et al., 2022). Most studies investigating microplastic pollution in birds are making use of dead individuals or invasive techniques and determine microplastic pollution e.g. in the proventriculus, gastrointestinal tract or the liver (Carlin et al., 2020; Weitzel et al., 2021; Teboul et al., 2021; Hoang and Mitten, 2022; Deoniziak et al., 2022; Navarro et al., 2023). In birds, it is also possible to analyse non-invasively collected samples, such as faecal samples, feather brushings or regurgitates (Reynolds and Ryan, 2018; Winkler et al., 2020; Le Guen et al., 2020; D'Souza et al., 2020; Nessi et al., 2022; Jeong et al., 2023). Whereas microplastic particles found on feathers or regurgitates have not entered the gastrointestinal tract of the birds (Carrillo et al., 2023), microplastic found in faeces are a better measure of relevant contamination levels, as the particles have already been digested and might have therefore affected the birds (de Souza et al., 2022). It has been shown that the number of excreted plastic particles is positively linked to the number of plastic particles in the gut (Provencher et al., 2018), for which faecal samples can be used as a non-invasive indicator of microplastic pollution in birds (Sherlock et al., 2022). Microplastic pollution is well-studied in birds of marine environments (Provencher et al., 2018; O'Hara et al., 2019; Le Guen et al., 2020; Bourdages et al., 2021; Teboul et al., 2021; Navarro et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Jeong et al., 2023), but less is known regarding the microplastic pollution of birds in freshwater ecosystems. Recent studies have shown that birds of freshwater ecosystems do ingest microplastics (Zhao et al., 2016; Gil-Delgado et al., 2017; Reynolds and Ryan, 2018; Brookson et al., 2019; Bilal et al., 2023), but few information is available regarding species-specific differences and ecological effects (Bhatt and Chauhan, 2023). On top of that, there is a lack of information regarding microplastic pollution of birds inhabiting urban freshwaters, where elevated pollution levels are found (Bhatt and Chauhan, 2023; Lee et al., 2024). Microplastic pollution levels in urban environments are so high that there are discussions to include the reduction of urban microplastic pollution to the UN Sustainable Development Goals (Lee et al., 2024). The aim of this study was to investigate microplastic pollution in wild birds inhabiting urban waterbodies, and to test for possible links between microplastic pollution and body condition. 2. Material and methods We collected faecal samples of free-flying birds at urban waters in the city of Münster, Germany, between December 2020 and March 2021. Individual birds were captured with clap-nets or hand-held dip nets. We marked all birds with an individually numbered metal ring, assessed their age (adult or first year) based on plumage characteristics (Demongin, 2016), and measured maximum wing length (in cm) as well as body mass (in g). Body condition (g/cm) was calculated by dividing body mass by wing length. Faecal samples were either collected when birds defecated during handling or when a marked individual was seen defecating, and its ring number read. Permissions to capture and ring birds were issued by the conservation authorities of North-Rhine Westphalia to WH, MM, and NN. All samples were stored in glass vials and frozen until examination in the laboratory. We weighed the faecal samples to the nearest mg (Secura 225D1S, Sartorius Lab Instruments GmbH & Co KG, Göttingen, Germany). To screen for microplastic particles, samples were thawed at room temperature and filtered through filter papers using tap water. Hereafter, the filtrate on the filter paper was spread out in a Petri dish under the stereoscope. Subsequently, the entire filter paper was searched for microplastic particles. Microplastic particles do not show any cellular structure and microplastic fibres should have a homogeneous colour and be consistent in thickness through the entire length (Hidalgo-Ruz et al., 2012). To check whether the particles found were microplastics, the “hot needle test” was applied (Silva et al., 2018; Lusher et al., 2020). For this purpose, a needle was heated with a lighter and held to the particle. If it began to melt and contract, we identified it as microplastic. Each particle was recorded individually, and its shape and colour noted. All particles found were collected in screw-cap vials. To correct for possible microplastic pollution through the tap water or laboratory air, we prepared a control for each sample (Prata et al., 2019). For this purpose, the same amount of tap water was filtered through filter paper and placed adjacent to the sample under the stereoscope for the time of investigation. These control samples were searched for microplastics under the stereoscope using the same procedure as for the faecal samples. fetched_contents.text: Critical review on microplastics in fecal matter: Research progress, analytical methods and future outlook Introduction Microplastics are emerging environmental pollutants that originate either from the disintegration of larger plastics via physical and biological degradation or from the applications of personal care products which contain microplastics that are primarily manufactured in specific smaller sizes (Koelmans and Pahl, 2019; Guerranti et al., 2019). The occurrence of microplastics has been noted in all of Earth's major ecosystems, including marine (Andrady, 2011), freshwater (Li et al., 2020), estuary (Han et al., 2020) and atmosphere (Chen et al., 2020). The slower degradation rate of microplastics in aquatic environments increases their persistence in the environment and their bioavailability to a wide range of organisms (Nelms et al., 2018; Caruso, 2019). There is currently numerous evidence of microplastic ingestion from low to high trophic organisms, including fish, shrimp, turtles, bivalves, zooplankton and whales (Abbasi et al., 2018; Hermabessiere et al., 2019; Duncan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020). The risks associated with the ingestion/retention of microplastics in organisms include substantial threats on growth and reproduction of organisms (De Sá et al., 2018). The ingested microplastics can be transferred to another organism via prey ingestion and thereby, gaining entry into the food web. Microplastics have been shown to act as a carrier of heavy metals and organic pollutants to environments and to organisms after ingestion (Caruso, 2019). While the uptake of microplastics by biota is becoming apparent, evidence from laboratory experiments started appearing as well for the egestion of microplastics in feces or solid biowastes (Jinhui et al., 2019; Moreschi et al., 2020). Many organisms utilize a natural process of expulsion of digestible and non-digestible material for eliminating the microplastics from their internal system in feces. Even mussels have shown to eliminate microplastics as pseudofeces (Woods et al., 2018). Inspired by these interesting findings, in recent years, a number of studies have examined excreta from low to high trophic organisms for understanding the extent of microplastics contamination in feces at ambient conditions and brought important information on concentration and characteristics of microplastics detected in feces (Zhao et al., 2018; Beriot et al., 2020; Moore et al., 2020; Provencher et al., 2018). Remarkably, Schwabl et al. (2019) published a comprehensive study demonstrating the presence of microplastics belonging to 9 different polymer types in human stool. Based on these contributions, it can be said that the phenomenon of microplastics expulsion is common across trophic organisms. At present, very little is known about the real-world behavioral implications of the microplastics in feces from being released into environment. However, it has been speculated that the frequency of occurrence and the number of plastic pieces packed in fecal matter may play a significant role when evaluating the potential harm of marine plastic litter. Despite the huge amount of effort and promising advances, one of the main issues related to microplastics research is the quantification and identification of microplastics and contaminations during this process. The constant increase in literature along with the variability in methodology that mediate particle separation, quantification and identification can lead to erroneous comparability of data and conclusions. That is because of the extensive development of analytical and characterization methods for providing fundamental information (e.g., concentration and polymer) on microplastics. Additionally, it is worth highlighting that the availability of completely different processes may not always be very compatible and will require systematic testing with different environment samples. This fundamental problem has driven the need for a standardization of methodologies and aroused great interest among researchers to combine the available data by enabling the path towards a feasible harmonization of different approaches and scientific communications. Importantly, due to the emerging interesting in this topic, many significant and exciting reviews have acquired knowledge of the detection and identification of microplastics in sample matrices like water, sediment, biota and food (Prata et al., 2019; Kutralam-Muniasamy et al., 2020; Fok et al., 2020; Shruti et al., 2021), taking a first step towards standardization of methodologies. Abstract Simple Summary The interest in wildlife research has increased in the last decades as more scientists work within a One Health framework that regards human, livestock and wildlife health as connected entities. To minimise the impact of research on wildlife, collecting samples with as little disturbance of the animals as possible is important. In our review, we assess the use of so-called non-invasive sampling and summarise which samples can be used successfully when carrying out research on wildlife diseases and health status. Our results show that interest in minimally invasive sampling has steadily increased since the 2010s. Topics able to employ these methods include disease research, but also stress and other hormone assessments, pollution studies, and dietary studies. At the moment, such methods are mainly used to collect samples from land mammals, however, they can also be used in a wide range of other animals. Ever more capable analytical methods will allow for an even wider use of such “animal-friendly” sampling methods. Abstract In the last decades, wildlife diseases and the health status of animal populations have gained increasing attention from the scientific community as part of a One Health framework. Furthermore, the need for non-invasive sampling methods with a minimal impact on wildlife has become paramount in complying with modern ethical standards and regulations, and to collect high-quality and unbiased data. We analysed the publication trends on non-invasive sampling in wildlife health and disease research and offer a comprehensive review on the different samples that can be collected non-invasively. We retrieved 272 articles spanning from 1998 to 2021, with a rapid increase in number from 2010. Thirty-nine percent of the papers were focussed on diseases, 58% on other health-related topics, and 3% on both. Stress and other physiological parameters were the most addressed research topics, followed by viruses, helminths, and bacterial infections. Terrestrial mammals accounted for 75% of all publications, and faeces were the most widely used sample. Our review of the sampling materials and collection methods highlights that, although the use of some types of samples for specific applications is now consolidated, others are perhaps still underutilised and new technologies may offer future opportunities for an even wider use of non-invasively collected samples. Introduction In the last decades, awareness of the importance of studying and monitoring disease in wild animal populations has steadily grown. The need for a One Health approach that integrates wildlife, human, and domestic animal health into a single framework is now widely recognised [1] and has gained further attention due to the recent SARS-CoV-2 pandemic [2]. In addition to their relevance as a source of pathogens that may spill over to humans and domestic animals, many wild species are currently threatened by emerging diseases (e.g., white-nose syndrome in bats [3], chytridiomycosis in amphibians [4], or Chlamydia infection in koalas [5]), making wildlife disease research paramount from a conservation perspective [6,7]. Additionally, the need for a more complete understanding of disease circulation in natural populations has sparked the interest of many researchers who are now investigating those intrinsic factors affecting host–pathogen dynamics such as the host physiological and immunological status [8,9,10,11]. In parallel to the growing interest in wildlife disease, attention towards animal welfare in research has been growing since the ’60s, when Russell and Burch [12] proposed the 3Rs principle. It aims to replace animal use in research whenever possible, reduce the numbers of animals employed, and to refine the methods to limit their pain and distress. This principle has been incorporated in several legislations (e.g., [13]) and is now widely applied to laboratory animals. Ethical advances in wildlife research have been comparably slower, but the need for the development of non-invasive methods to safeguard animal welfare and avoid taking valuable animals from vulnerable populations is being advocated by several authors [14,15,16]. Wildlife disease and health surveys often rely on the opportunistic sampling of carcasses, and this is certainly an important resource for passive disease surveillance (e.g., [17,18,19,20] in the present Special Issue), but it can introduce relevant biases into epidemiological studies [21]. Random sampling of living individuals should therefore be preferred whenever researchers are interested in studying disease circulation in natural populations [22]. However, sampling living, free-ranging animals is a challenging endeavour, and biologists and veterinarians need to cope with several issues particular to the field that are not encountered when working with domestic or laboratory animals [23]. First and foremost, relevant constraints are related to logistics, as field work is often carried out in inaccessible locations, far away from laboratory facilities, making sample storage and transport a major concern. Another issue is related to capture and handling: capturing wild animals is normally work-demanding and indeed represents a source of distress for the animal, possibly altering physiological parameters [11] and posing ethical problems. Hence, a sampling method for wildlife should ideally be non-invasive, possibly require no trapping and/or handling to limit distress (although for some species this might be unavoidable) and be feasible in field conditions. Bird banding improves study efficiency and breadth by enabling repeated sampling of the same individual over time, improving identification and population-level inference, but it has important limits for studying microplastic ingestion.

First, banding enables repeated sampling of the same individual over time because it attaches a unique identifying number to a bird’s leg, allowing researchers to recognize a bird when it is recaptured or resighted later. This means the same bird can be monitored across seasons, years, or even decades, creating a longitudinal dataset rather than a one-off snapshot. The evidence shows that bird banding is one of the oldest and most important techniques used for studying and identifying individual birds [N3-R3], and that fecal samples linked to a bird’s band number can be used for dietary, disease, movement, or genetic studies [N1-R5]. This longitudinal tracking is a major efficiency gain because it allows researchers to study long-term changes in behavior, survival, or exposure without repeatedly capturing the same bird each time.

Second, banding improves identification and population-level inference by allowing individual identification and linking that to broader ecological patterns. Because each bird is uniquely banded, researchers can track movement, population size, migration patterns, disease spread, lifespan, and other population-level traits [N3-R1]. This is especially valuable for studies aiming to infer how a population responds to environmental stressors over time. The evidence also emphasizes that banding is used to track movement and survival of individual birds [N3-R4], which is directly relevant to interpreting exposure patterns across a population. Because banding can be combined with other data collected during capture, such as age, sex, or location, it supports more robust inference about population structure and dynamics [N1-R1][N1-R4].

Third, there are limits to using banding data to study microplastic ingestion. The evidence here is not direct, but the broader methodological context suggests that banding alone cannot reveal ingestion unless paired with a separate sampling method. Banding is a tracking and identification tool, not a direct measure of internal exposure; therefore, it is most useful for linking microplastic exposure to movement patterns, recapture locations, or population-level trends, rather than for measuring the actual presence of microplastics in a bird’s body. The evidence also notes that fecal samples collected during bird ringing/banding can be used as indicators of microplastic pollution [N2-R1], which implies that banding is most helpful when combined with fecal sampling rather than as a standalone method for ingestion detection. So, banding increases study efficiency and breadth by enabling repeated sampling and population-level inference, but it does not directly detect microplastic ingestion on its own [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].

Fecal analysis improves study efficiency and breadth by reducing handling stress and invasiveness, collecting data from many individuals quickly, and detecting microplastics even when ingestion is intermittent.

First, fecal sampling reduces handling stress and invasiveness because it is a non-invasive method that avoids direct capture, handling, or physical intrusion into the bird’s body. The evidence states that non-invasive sampling methods include collection approaches that do not require capture or cause disturbance to the animal [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It also emphasizes that non-invasive sampling is increasingly used in wildlife disease and health research because it minimizes impact on wildlife and is compatible with modern ethical standards [N6-F4]. In the context of bird studies, fecal samples can be collected without trapping the bird, which lowers stress and disturbance [N1-R3][N1-R5]. The review further explains that non-invasive sampling is especially valuable when researchers want to collect data with minimal disturbance, especially for species that are difficult to handle or for studies involving large numbers of individuals [N6-F4]. This makes fecal sampling highly efficient for wildlife studies where repeated handling would be impractical or harmful.

Second, fecal analysis can collect data from many individuals quickly because it is scalable and can be done on a large number of birds simultaneously. Non-invasive sampling is described as a powerful tool for population monitoring because it can be used on many individuals without requiring extensive capture or handling [N6-R4]. The same review notes that faeces are the most widely used non-invasive sample type across wildlife species [N6-F4]. In bird studies, fecal samples are collected during ringing/banding or when birds defecate during handling, allowing researchers to obtain samples from many individuals in a relatively short time frame [N2-F1]. The evidence also shows that fecal samples can be stored rapidly and processed later, which supports efficient field logistics and data collection [N1-R3][N6-F4]. This scalability is a major efficiency gain for studies with broad taxonomic or spatial coverage.

Third, fecal analysis can detect microplastics even when ingestion is intermittent because microplastics that have been digested and excreted are more directly relevant to contamination levels than particles on feathers or regurgitates. The evidence states that microplastics found in faeces are a better measure of relevant contamination levels because the particles have already been digested and might have therefore affected the birds [N2-F1]. It also explains that the number of excreted plastic particles is positively linked to the number of plastic particles in the gut [N2-F1], supporting the idea that fecal samples can reflect intermittent or variable ingestion. The same source notes that fecal samples collected during bird ringing/banding can be used as indicators of microplastic pollution [N2-R1], which means they are especially useful for detecting contamination patterns even when individual birds do not consistently ingest microplastics [N2-F1][N2-R1]. This makes fecal analysis a strong complement to more invasive methods because it can capture exposure events that are not captured in one-off captures.

Overall, fecal analysis enhances efficiency and breadth by being less stressful, more scalable, and better suited to detecting microplastic contamination even when ingestion is variable or intermittent [N1-R3][N2-F1][N6-F4].

Combined banding plus fecal analysis increases methodological value by complementing each other in tracking exposure and behavior, by being suited to different questions, and by increasing the breadth of species and locations sampled.

First, banding and fecal sampling complement each other in tracking exposure and behavior. Banding provides individual identification and movement information, while fecal sampling provides exposure data. The evidence shows that bird banding is used to track movement and survival of individual birds [N3-R4], and that fecal samples collected during ringing/banding can be used as indicators of microplastic pollution [N2-R1]. Together, this means researchers can link a bird’s behavior, location, and recapture history to its exposure status. For example, a bird that is captured, banded, and later recaptured at a different site can be matched to its fecal sample, allowing researchers to ask whether microplastic exposure varies with habitat or movement patterns [N1-R5][N2-R1]. This combination is especially valuable because banding provides the temporal and spatial context that fecal analysis alone cannot provide.

Second, each method is best suited to different questions. Banding is best suited to questions about individual identity, population dynamics, movement, and long-term tracking [N3-R1][N3-R4]. Fecal analysis is best suited to questions about exposure, contamination levels, diet, and non-invasive assessment of microplastics or other physiological indicators [N1-R5][N2-F1][N6-R2]. In microplastic studies, banding helps researchers identify the same individual repeatedly, while fecal sampling helps determine whether and how much microplastic that individual has ingested [N2-R1][N2-F1]. This division of labor means the combined approach can address both who the birds are and what they have been exposed to.

Third, combined use increases the breadth of species and locations sampled. Banding is often used across a wide range of species and sites, and fecal sampling can be collected non-invasively during banding events, making it easier to sample birds that are difficult to handle or monitor directly. The evidence shows that fecal sampling can be done during bird ringing/banding, which supports broad taxonomic coverage [N1-R5][N2-R1]. It also notes that non-invasive sampling is being used in a wide range of animals, including terrestrial mammals, and that it can be applied in inaccessible or hard-to-reach areas [N6-F4]. In the terrestrial bird context, one study explicitly combines banding and fecal sampling to measure microplastic loading in small terrestrial birds, showing that this approach can be used across species and locations [N5-F2]. This breadth is important because microplastic ingestion can vary by species, habitat, and geography, and combined banding- fecal sampling allows researchers to collect comparable data across diverse settings [N5-F2][N2-F1].

In summary, banding plus fecal analysis is a complementary methodological pair: banding tracks individuals and movement, fecal sampling measures exposure and contamination, and together they support broader, more informative studies of microplastic ingestion [N3-R4][N2-R1][N5-F2].

Microplastic ingestion biology affects fecal detection and interpretation in several ways: whether microplastics appear in feces versus other tissues depends on digestion and transit, gut transit time and excretion shape fecal detection, and contamination and false-positive risks exist in fecal microplastic studies.

First, whether microplastics appear in feces versus other tissues depends on whether they have been ingested, retained, or digested. The evidence shows that microplastics found in feces are a better measure of relevant contamination levels because the particles have already been digested and might have therefore affected the birds [N2-F1]. It also notes that the number of excreted plastic particles is positively linked to the number of plastic particles in the gut [N2-F1]. This means fecal detection is a downstream indicator of ingestion rather than a direct measure of exposure in the environment or in the digestive tract. In other words, feces are more informative about internal exposure after digestion, whereas other tissues or regurgitates may reflect external contact or incomplete digestion [N2-F1][N2-R1].

Second, digestion, gut transit time, and excretion shape fecal detection. The review on microplastics in fecal matter explains that digestion is the most commonly used approach for microplastic separation, and that microplastics can be expelled through feces or solid biowastes after ingestion [N4-F3]. It further notes that many organisms use natural processes to expel digestible and non-digestible material, and that the excretion process can result in microplastics appearing in feces [N4-F3]. The same source emphasizes that the timing and route of excretion are important because they determine whether microplastics are detected in feces rather than in other tissues or organs [N4-F3]. The evidence also highlights that microplastics can alter gut permeability and digestion, which can affect how they move through the gut and whether they are excreted [N4-R4]. In birds, this implies that fecal detection depends on both the bird’s digestion and the speed with which microplastics pass through the gastrointestinal tract [N2-F1][N4-F3].

Third, contamination and false-positive risks exist in fecal microplastic studies. The evidence notes that microplastics in feces can act as a vector for environmental contaminants or plastic additives that may leach out [N4-R5]. It also explains that contamination during sampling and analytical procedures can introduce errors, and that contamination and identification biases are a major issue in microplastic research [N4-F3]. The review further states that the constant increase in literature along with variability in methodology can lead to erroneous comparability of data and conclusions [N4-F3]. In the bird fecal context, the study explicitly mentions that controls are used to correct for microplastic pollution through tap water or laboratory air, which indicates that contamination is a recognized and active problem [N2-F1]. This means fecal microplastic studies must carefully distinguish true ingestion from contamination, false positives, and methodological artifacts [N4-F3][N4-R5][N2-F1].

In total, microplastic ingestion biology affects fecal detection and interpretation by determining whether particles reach feces at all, by shaping transit time and excretion, and by creating contamination and false-positive risks that must be controlled [N2-F1][N4-F3][N4-R4][N4-R5].

## How bird banding and fecal analysis enhance the efficiency and breadth of studies investigating microplastic ingestion in terrestrial birds

Bird banding and fecal analysis together enhance microplastic ingestion studies by combining the strengths of individual tracking with non-invasive exposure measurement. Banding improves efficiency and breadth through repeated sampling over time and population-level inference, while fecal analysis improves efficiency and breadth through low handling stress, scalability, and sensitivity to contamination exposure. Their combination also allows researchers to track behavior and exposure together, ask different types of questions, and broaden the range of species and locations that can be studied [N8][N9][N11][N10].

## 1) Banding improves study efficiency and breadth

This is especially valuable for studies aiming to understand how populations respond to environmental stressors over time. Banding can also be combined with other capture data, such as age, sex, or location, to support more robust population-level analysis [N1-R1][N1-R4].

However, banding has important limits for studying microplastic ingestion directly. Banding itself does not detect microplastics in the body; it is a tracking and identification tool. The evidence suggests that fecal samples collected during bird ringing/banding are useful as indicators of microplastic pollution, which implies that banding is most helpful when combined with fecal sampling rather than as a standalone ingestion-detection method [N2-R1]. So, banding enhances efficiency and breadth by enabling repeated sampling and population-level inference, but it does not by itself reveal ingestion [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].

## 2) Fecal analysis improves study efficiency and breadth

Fecal analysis improves efficiency and breadth by reducing handling stress and invasiveness. It is a non-invasive method that avoids direct capture, handling, or physical intrusion into the bird’s body [N6-R2][N6-R3]. Non-invasive sampling is increasingly used in wildlife disease and health research because it minimizes impact on wildlife and aligns with modern ethical standards [N6-F4]. This makes fecal sampling especially efficient for studies involving large numbers of individuals or difficult-to-handle species [N6-F4].

Non-invasive sampling is described as a powerful tool for population monitoring, and faeces are the most widely used non-invasive sample type across wildlife species [N6-R4][N6-F4]. In bird studies, fecal samples can be collected during ringing/banding or when birds defecate during handling, allowing researchers to obtain samples from many individuals in a relatively short time frame [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that fecal samples can be stored rapidly and processed later, supporting efficient field logistics [N1-R3][N6-F4]. This scalability is a major efficiency gain for studies with broad taxonomic or spatial coverage.

A third efficiency benefit is that fecal analysis can detect microplastics even when ingestion is intermittent. The evidence states that microplastics found in feces are a better measure of relevant contamination levels because the particles have already been digested and might have therefore affected the birds [N2-F1]. It also explains that the number of excreted plastic particles is positively linked to the number of plastic particles in the gut, supporting the idea that fecal samples can reflect variable or intermittent ingestion [N2-F1]. The same source notes that fecal samples collected during bird ringing/banding can be used as indicators of microplastic pollution, which means they are especially useful for detecting contamination patterns even when individual birds do not consistently ingest microplastics [N2-R1]. This makes fecal analysis a strong complement to more invasive methods because it can capture exposure events that are not captured in one-off captures [N1-R3][N2-F1][N6-F4].

---

## 3) Microplastic ingestion biology affects fecal detection and interpretation

The biology of microplastic ingestion directly shapes how fecal detection and interpretation work. First, whether microplastics appear in feces versus other tissues depends on whether they have been ingested, retained, or digested. The evidence shows that microplastics found in feces are a better measure of relevant contamination levels because the particles have already been digested and might have therefore affected the birds [N2-F1]. It also notes that the number of excreted plastic particles is positively linked to the number of plastic particles in the gut, meaning fecal detection is a downstream indicator of ingestion rather than a direct measure of exposure in the environment or in the digestive tract [N2-F1].

Second, digestion, gut transit time, and excretion shape fecal detection. The review on microplastics in fecal matter explains that digestion is the most commonly used approach for microplastic separation, and that microplastics can be expelled through feces or solid biowastes after ingestion [N4-F3]. It further notes that many organisms use natural processes to expel digestible and non-digestible material, and that the excretion process can result in microplastics appearing in feces [N4-F3]. The evidence also highlights that microplastics can alter gut permeability and digestion, which can affect how they move through the gut and whether they are excreted [N4-R4]. The evidence notes that microplastics in feces can act as a vector for environmental contaminants or plastic additives that may leach out [N4-R5]. It also explains that contamination during sampling and analytical procedures can introduce errors, and that contamination and identification biases are a major issue in microplastic research [N4-F3]. The review further states that the constant increase in literature along with variability in methodology can lead to erroneous comparability of data and conclusions [N4-F3]. Banding and fecal analysis complement each other in tracking exposure and behavior. Banding provides individual identification and movement information, while fecal sampling provides exposure data. This division of labor means the combined approach can address both who the birds are and what they have been exposed to [N3-R4][N2-F1].

Banding is often used across a wide range of species and sites, and fecal sampling can be collected non-invasively during banding events, making it easier to sample birds that are difficult to handle or monitor directly. ---

## Conclusion

Bird banding and fecal analysis together enhance the efficiency and breadth of microplastic ingestion studies in terrestrial birds by providing complementary strengths: banding enables repeated sampling, identification, and population-level inference, while fecal analysis provides non-invasive, scalable, and contamination-sensitive exposure measurement [N8][N9][N11][N10]. Their combination also improves tracking of exposure and behavior, allows researchers to ask different types of questions, and broadens the range of species and locations that can be studied [N11]. However, fecal microplastic studies remain sensitive to digestion, transit, contamination, and false-positive risks, so careful methodology and controls are essential [N10]. Overall, these two methods together make microplastic ingestion studies more efficient, more broadly applicable, and more informative [N8][N9][N11][N10].

## How bird banding and fecal analysis enhance the efficiency and breadth of studies investigating microplastic ingestion in terrestrial birds

Bird banding and fecal analysis together enhance microplastic ingestion studies by combining the strengths of individual tracking with non-invasive exposure measurement. Banding improves efficiency and breadth through repeated sampling over time and population-level inference, while fecal analysis improves efficiency and breadth through low handling stress, scalability, and sensitivity to contamination exposure. Their combination also allows researchers to track behavior and exposure together, ask different types of questions, and broaden the range of species and locations that can be studied [N8][N9][N11][N10].

---

## 1) Banding improves study efficiency and breadth

Bird banding is a core method for long-term wildlife monitoring because it attaches a unique identifying number to a bird’s leg, enabling repeated sampling of the same individual over time. This longitudinal tracking means researchers can follow a bird across seasons, years, or even decades, creating a dataset that is richer than a single capture event [N8]. The evidence shows that bird banding is one of the oldest and most important techniques used for studying and identifying individual birds [N3-R3], and that fecal samples linked to a bird’s band number can be used for dietary, disease, movement, or genetic studies [N1-R5].

This repeated sampling also improves identification and population-level inference. Because each bird is uniquely banded, researchers can track movement, population size, migration patterns, disease spread, lifespan, and other population traits [N3-R1][N3-R4]. This is especially valuable for studies aiming to understand how populations respond to environmental stressors over time. Banding can also be combined with other capture data, such as age, sex, or location, to support more robust population-level analysis [N1-R1][N1-R4].

However, banding has important limits for studying microplastic ingestion directly. Banding itself does not detect microplastics in the body; it is a tracking and identification tool. The evidence suggests that fecal samples collected during bird ringing/banding are useful as indicators of microplastic pollution, which implies that banding is most helpful when combined with fecal sampling rather than as a standalone ingestion-detection method [N2-R1]. So, banding enhances efficiency and breadth by enabling repeated sampling and population-level inference, but it does not by itself reveal ingestion [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].

---

## 2) Fecal analysis improves study efficiency and breadth

Fecal analysis improves efficiency and breadth by reducing handling stress and invasiveness. It is a non-invasive method that avoids direct capture, handling, or physical intrusion into the bird’s body [N6-R2][N6-R3]. Non-invasive sampling is increasingly used in wildlife disease and health research because it minimizes impact on wildlife and aligns with modern ethical standards [N6-F4]. In the bird context, fecal samples can be collected without trapping the bird, which lowers stress and disturbance [N1-R3][N1-R5]. This makes fecal sampling especially efficient for studies involving large numbers of individuals or difficult-to-handle species [N6-F4].

Fecal analysis also increases breadth because it can collect data from many individuals quickly. Non-invasive sampling is described as a powerful tool for population monitoring, and faeces are the most widely used non-invasive sample type across wildlife species [N6-R4][N6-F4]. In bird studies, fecal samples can be collected during ringing/banding or when birds defecate during handling, allowing researchers to obtain samples from many individuals in a relatively short time frame [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that fecal samples can be stored rapidly and processed later, supporting efficient field logistics [N1-R3][N6-F4]. This scalability is a major efficiency gain for studies with broad taxonomic or spatial coverage.

A third efficiency benefit is that fecal analysis can detect microplastics even when ingestion is intermittent. The evidence states that microplastics found in feces are a better measure of relevant contamination levels because the particles have already been digested and might have therefore affected the birds [N2-F1]. It also explains that the number of excreted plastic particles is positively linked to the number of plastic particles in the gut, supporting the idea that fecal samples can reflect variable or intermittent ingestion [N2-F1]. The same source notes that fecal samples collected during bird ringing/banding can be used as indicators of microplastic pollution, which means they are especially useful for detecting contamination patterns even when individual birds do not consistently ingest microplastics [N2-R1]. This makes fecal analysis a strong complement to more invasive methods because it can capture exposure events that are not captured in one-off captures [N1-R3][N2-F1][N6-F4].

---

## 3) Microplastic ingestion biology affects fecal detection and interpretation

The biology of microplastic ingestion directly shapes how fecal detection and interpretation work. First, whether microplastics appear in feces versus other tissues depends on whether they have been ingested, retained, or digested. The evidence shows that microplastics found in feces are a better measure of relevant contamination levels because the particles have already been digested and might have therefore affected the birds [N2-F1]. It also notes that the number of excreted plastic particles is positively linked to the number of plastic particles in the gut, meaning fecal detection is a downstream indicator of ingestion rather than a direct measure of exposure in the environment or in the digestive tract [N2-F1].

Second, digestion, gut transit time, and excretion shape fecal detection. The review on microplastics in fecal matter explains that digestion is the most commonly used approach for microplastic separation, and that microplastics can be expelled through feces or solid biowastes after ingestion [N4-F3]. It further notes that many organisms use natural processes to expel digestible and non-digestible material, and that the excretion process can result in microplastics appearing in feces [N4-F3]. The evidence also highlights that microplastics can alter gut permeability and digestion, which can affect how they move through the gut and whether they are excreted [N4-R4]. In birds, this means fecal detection depends on both the bird’s digestion and the speed with which microplastics pass through the gastrointestinal tract [N2-F1][N4-F3].

Third, contamination and false-positive risks exist in fecal microplastic studies. The evidence notes that microplastics in feces can act as a vector for environmental contaminants or plastic additives that may leach out [N4-R5]. It also explains that contamination during sampling and analytical procedures can introduce errors, and that contamination and identification biases are a major issue in microplastic research [N4-F3]. The review further states that the constant increase in literature along with variability in methodology can lead to erroneous comparability of data and conclusions [N4-F3]. In the bird fecal context, the study explicitly mentions that controls are used to correct for microplastic pollution through tap water or laboratory air, which indicates that contamination is a recognized and active problem [N2-F1]. This means fecal microplastic studies must carefully distinguish true ingestion from contamination, false positives, and methodological artifacts [N4-F3][N4-R5][N2-F1].

---

## 4) Combined methodological value of banding plus fecal analysis

Banding and fecal analysis complement each other in tracking exposure and behavior. Banding provides individual identification and movement information, while fecal sampling provides exposure data. The evidence shows that bird banding is used to track movement and survival of individual birds [N3-R4], and that fecal samples collected during ringing/banding can be used as indicators of microplastic pollution [N2-R1]. Together, this means researchers can link a bird’s behavior, location, and recapture history to its exposure status. For example, a bird that is captured, banded, and later recaptured at a different site can be matched to its fecal sample, allowing researchers to ask whether microplastic exposure varies with habitat or movement patterns [N1-R5][N2-R1].

Each method is best suited to different questions. Banding is best suited to questions about individual identity, population dynamics, movement, and long-term tracking [N3-R1][N3-R4]. Fecal analysis is best suited to questions about exposure, contamination levels, diet, and non-invasive assessment of microplastics or other physiological indicators [N1-R5][N2-F1][N6-R2]. In microplastic studies, banding helps researchers identify the same individual repeatedly, while fecal sampling helps determine whether and how much microplastic that individual has ingested [N2-R1][N2-F1]. This division of labor means the combined approach can address both who the birds are and what they have been exposed to [N3-R4][N2-F1].

Combined use also increases the breadth of species and locations sampled. Banding is often used across a wide range of species and sites, and fecal sampling can be collected non-invasively during banding events, making it easier to sample birds that are difficult to handle or monitor directly. The evidence shows that fecal sampling can be done during bird ringing/banding, which supports broad taxonomic coverage [N1-R5][N2-R1]. It also notes that non-invasive sampling is being used in a wide range of animals, including terrestrial mammals, and that it can be applied in inaccessible or hard-to-reach areas [N6-F4]. In the terrestrial bird context, one study explicitly combines banding and fecal sampling to measure microplastic loading in small terrestrial birds, showing that this approach can be used across species and locations [N5-F2]. This breadth is important because microplastic ingestion can vary by species, habitat, and geography, and combined banding-fecal sampling allows researchers to collect comparable data across diverse settings [N5-F2][N2-F1].

---

## Conclusion

Bird banding and fecal analysis together enhance the efficiency and breadth of microplastic ingestion studies in terrestrial birds by providing complementary strengths: banding enables repeated sampling, identification, and population-level inference, while fecal analysis provides non-invasive, scalable, and contamination-sensitive exposure measurement [N8][N9][N11][N10]. Their combination also improves tracking of exposure and behavior, allows researchers to ask different types of questions, and broadens the range of species and locations that can be studied [N11]. However, fecal microplastic studies remain sensitive to digestion, transit, contamination, and false-positive risks, so careful methodology and controls are essential [N10]. Overall, these two methods together make microplastic ingestion studies more efficient, more broadly applicable, and more informative [N8][N9][N11][N10].
